title: Three ways to say "have"
goal: Choose between کے پاس، کا، and میں — three patterns of possession that English squeezes into the single word "have".
bekal: using کے پاس for things you can carry around
using the possessive form for relatives and body parts
saying that something is in a place

notes: **Urdu has no verb "to have" at all.** All it has is ہونا ("to be") plus the right word for place or possession. That's why there are three patterns, and picking the wrong one doesn't make a grammar mistake so much as a **change in meaning**.

**Things you can carry around use کے پاس.** میرے پاس کتاب ہے = "I have a book", literally "near me is a book". Money, books, time, a car, a phone, keys — all work this way. The forms: میرے پاس، تمہارے پاس، آپ کے پاس، اس کے پاس، ہمارے پاس، ان کے پاس.

**Relatives and body parts use the ordinary possessive.** میرا بھائی ہے ("I have a brother"), اس کی دو بہنیں ہیں ("she has two sisters"). Saying میرے پاس بھائی ہے would sound as if your brother were an object you carry around — and Pakistanis would laugh.

**Things fixed to a place use میں or پر.** گھر میں انٹرنیٹ ہے ("there's internet in the house"), کمرے میں الماری ہے ("there's a wardrobe in the room"). For buildings, cities, and rooms, this is the right pattern — not کے پاس.

**The word اپنا means "one's own", and it's required when the owner is the subject of the sentence.** میں اپنا کمرہ صاف کرتا ہوں = "I clean my (own) room". Using میرا there — میں میرا کمرہ — is a mistake people hear immediately. The rule is simple: if the owner is already the subject, switch to اپنا.

**Qualities and states use the possessive too.** For example آپ کا چہرہ ایماندار ہے · میری طبیعت ٹھیک نہیں ("I'm not feeling well") · اس کا مزاج اچھا ہے ("he has a good temper"). This group belongs with relatives and body parts.

grammars.title: Three patterns, and how to choose
body: Ask yourself: **could you put this thing in a bag?** If yes, کے پاس. If it's part of you or your family, the ordinary possessive. If it's fixed to a place, میں or پر.

Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: There's a book on the table.

after: ⚠️ One group often causes doubt: **illnesses and symptoms**. They use کو, not either pattern above: مجھے بخار ہے ("I have a fever"), مجھے زکام ہے ("I have a cold"). This is the dative sentence from unit 10, and unit 18 covers it more fully.

grammars.title: One's own: اپنا
body: Urdu has a special possessive word used when the owner is **the same as the subject of the sentence**. English has no exact equivalent, but Russian, Sanskrit, and Turkish do — and the rule is the same in all of them.

head: Wrong
Right
Meaning
rows: وہ اس کی کتاب پڑھتی ہے
We go home to our house.

after: The last row shows why this rule matters: اپنی and اس کی tell you **whose book** it is. With اپنی, the book is her own; with اس کی, it belongs to someone else. English has to add "own" — or leave it ambiguous; Urdu separates them in the pronoun itself.
The form follows the thing owned, as usual: اپنا (m sg), اپنی (f), اپنے (m pl & before a postposition).

blocks.title: Ten everyday sentences about having
items: Things: میرے پاس پیسے نہیں ہیں۔ ("I don't have any money") · آپ کے پاس چابی ہے؟ ("do you have the key?") · میرے پاس وقت نہیں ہے۔ ("I don't have time")
Relatives: میرے دو بھائی ہیں۔ ("I have two brothers") · اس کا کوئی بچہ نہیں ہے۔ ("he has no children")
Places: اس کمرے میں پنکھا ہے؟ ("is there a fan in this room?") · گھر میں کوئی نہیں ہے۔ ("there's nobody at home")
One's own: میں اپنے کمرے میں پڑھتا ہوں۔ ("I study in my own room") · اپنا خیال رکھیے۔ ("take care of yourself") — this last one is a warm and very common way to say goodbye.
